summary: Fund

Pabrai Wagons ETF, ticker WAGN, NYSE Arca (it began trading on the NYSE on Feb 9, 2026 ; a June 18, 2026 release announced the move to NYSE Arca). Actively managed, long-only, non-diversified. CUSIP 74316P538.
Manager

Mohnish Pabrai is the sole portfolio manager. The adviser is Dhandho Funds LLC, doing business as Pabrai Wagons Advisors, in West Lake Hills, Texas. The prospectus says the fund depends on him and would have to liquidate without him.
Objective

Long-term capital appreciation: a concentrated portfolio of high-quality businesses bought at a meaningful discount to intrinsic value and held for many years. No geographic or industry limits; up to 100% outside the US, including emerging and frontier markets.
History

Started as the Pabrai Wagons Fund, a mutual fund, on Sep 29, 2023. It converted into the ETF on Feb 6, 2026 (first ETF trade Feb 9) and carries the mutual fund's Institutional Class performance history. The ETF replaced share classes costing 1.25% (retail) and 1.00% (institutional) net.
Fee
0.90% a year, a single flat fee. The adviser pays most operating costs. Brokerage costs, taxes, borrowing interest and acquired-fund fees are excluded. There is no 12b-1 fee and no performance fee.
Size
About $298 million in early November 2026 (the fact sheet shows $313.0 million at its reporting date). Pabrai's firms manage $1.4 billion in total across the private funds and the ETF.
Holdings

20 positions. The top 10 are 67.4% of assets (Oct 31, 2026): Reysas REIT 14.9%, Transocean 9.2%, Warrior Met Coal 7.0%, Edelweiss 5.9%, Gimat 5.8%, Valaris 5.6%, Noble 5.0%, TAV Airports 4.8%, Odfjell Drilling 4.7%, Constellation Software 4.5%. The fund reports zero overlap with the S&P 500.
Sectors

Energy 24.7%, Real Estate 14.9%, Information Technology 14.3%, Financials 13.6%, Industrials 12.3%, Materials 11.4%, Consumer Staples 5.8%, Consumer Discretionary 2.9%, cash 0.2% (Oct 31, 2026). At June 30, 2026 the country split was Turkey 29.7%, US 23.1%, India 13.7%, Switzerland 9.5%, Canada 8.9%, Kazakhstan 4.9%.
Turnover
40% for the year to June 30, 2026 (69.25% the year before).
Shareholders

Held mostly through brokers. As of Oct 7, 2026 record holders over 5%: Charles Schwab 23.81%, National Financial Services 19.32%, Vanguard Brokerage 17.69%, Interactive Brokers 10.12%, Stifel 6.94%, Pershing 5.03%.

p: WAGN is the exchange-traded successor to the Pabrai Wagons Fund. The board approved the reorganization on Nov 18, 2025, and shareholders did not need to vote. It closed around Feb 6, 2026. The stated reasons were reaching more investors, greater tax efficiency from in-kind redemptions, intraday trading, lower expected total expenses and daily holdings transparency. The ETF also dropped the mutual fund's 1.00% fee on shares sold within 90 days.

The 0.90% single fee compares with 1.25% (retail) and 1.00% (institutional) net, and 1.84% and 1.59% gross, at the old mutual fund. On $10,000 the prospectus shows $92 for one year and $1,108 over ten at a 5% assumed return. In the year to June 30, 2025 the adviser had been waiving part of its fee to keep expenses at the cap; in fiscal 2026 the fund's reported expense ratio was 0.94% after a waiver and 1.08% before it, and the net advisory fee was $876,703 after a $253,408 waiver.

Shares are created and redeemed only in blocks of 10,000 by authorized participants, so the price on the exchange can drift away from net asset value (NAV). The prospectus lists that as a risk and says the fund's website carries daily premium and discount data.

The record is short and uneven. The mutual fund lost 13.29% in the year to June 30, 2025, gained 3.98% in calendar 2025 against 17.88% for the S&P 500, and then did sharply better after the ETF launch: 28.90% for the year to June 30, 2026 against 22.32% for the index, and 30.14% for 2026 through Oct 31 against 11.77%.

Even so, since inception on Sep 29, 2023 the fund trails the index: 16.91% a year at Oct 31, 2026 against 21.83%. The June 2026 shareholder report says so directly: the since-inception returns 'continue to trail the S&P 500'. Monthly swings are large (+13.8% in August 2026, then about -8.2% in September).
Market-price returns have run slightly ahead of NAV returns at every reported date (table above), so the shares' premium to NAV is a bit wider than at the start of 2026.

The June 2026 report groups about 78% of the portfolio into six themes: offshore oil services (18%), financial services in India (14%), the 'Mark Leonard complex' of Constellation Software-related companies in Canada and Europe (14%), metallurgical coal in the US (14%), the Reysas group in Turkey (9%) and TAV Airports in Turkey (9%).

By Oct 31, 2026 the top ten were 67.4% of assets. Energy was 24.7%, real estate 14.9% (almost all Reysas REIT), and the fund held nothing in the S&P 500. Since March 31, 2026 the fund added Odfjell Drilling and Odfjell Technology (Norway), and Mongolian Mining dropped out of the holdings list.

Valuation claims come from the sponsor's own investor presentation and are not independently checked. For example: Reysas, over $3 billion of liquidation value against a market value of about $2.1 billion; Transocean, a 2–3x return in the downside case; Warrior Met Coal, a 9% free cash flow yield; Kaspi, worth 2–3x its market cap even if its Turkey expansion fails; Gimat, a Turkish wholesale-club chain with two stores today and 'significant execution risk'.

commentary.h: What Pabrai told shareholders on the calls
p: Aug 20, 2025 call: the fund was about $80 million and would turn profitable for the adviser at about $150 million. He said no fee increase was planned and fees could fall as assets grow. He admitted the fund had badly underperformed the S&P 500 in its first two years and argued many holdings need five years or more to pay off, pointing to Reysas, held since 2019, which showed little return for three or four years. He explained most of the early turnover by launch timing and the sizing of Edelweiss (about 20%) and offshore drillers (about 12%). He expects only two or three new ideas a year. He said trades are allocated on a compliance-approved rotation: the Wagons fund gets priority every fifth day, and the three private funds the other days.

Dec 3, 2025 call: the fund passed $100 million that day, and he announced the ETF conversion. He called Edelweiss the largest position (about 18–19%) with several more subsidiary IPOs planned, described Warrior Met Coal (13–15% of the fund) as one of the lowest-cost seaborne producers, and added Gimat, where his funds own more than 20%. He rejected Penske Automotive as too expensive and listed Toll Brothers, Pulte and Occidental among his lowest-conviction bets. He said mutual fund rules force more positions than he would hold in his private funds, which he does not see as a big penalty.

June 10, 2026 shareholder meeting: mostly detailed holding by holding discussion. He called Constellation Software the best-managed holding and said the Kaspi dividend yield is around 10%. On the offshore drillers (over 19% together) he argued that capital intensity does not make a business bad if bought well below asset value, and that Transocean and Valaris is a 'win-win' deal. TAV Airports was down about 30% in dollars over two years because of engine groundings, Boeing delays and low airport fees, and he stayed bullish. He said he no longer sells just because a stock nears intrinsic value, and has no rule forcing him to trim winners. Fund-level performance, premiums and fees were not discussed in that transcript.
I could not open the Sept 23, 2026 and March 11, 2026 transcripts, so they are not summarized here. The replay pages for those calls show the performance tables used above.

Key man: the fund depends on Pabrai and would have to liquidate without him. Non-diversified and concentrated. Foreign and emerging-market exposure, with Turkey (lira volatility, a large current account deficit, political risk) and India (government influence, family-controlled companies, illiquidity, and tax accruals on capital gains that reduce NAV) both named. Sector emphasis of 25% or more in one sector is permitted. Cash can be large for long periods. ETF-specific risks: few authorized participants, cash redemptions, and the chance of material discounts to NAV.

commentary.h: Conflicts and incentives to know about
p: Pabrai also runs private funds through Dalal Street LLC, which pay him performance fees. The adviser's own filing says this creates an incentive to direct the best ideas to the performance-fee accounts, and that trades are allocated pro rata by procedure. The ETF itself pays no performance fee. Pabrai receives no salary from the adviser; he is part owner and gets distributions based on firm profits, plus pay from Dalal Street.

stake.answer: Almost nothing, in the ETF itself. The fund's Statement of Additional Information (dated Oct 31, 2026) reports Mohnish Pabrai's ownership in the fund as $1–$10,000 as of June 30, 2026. That is the lowest range the form offers. A year earlier, for the mutual fund, it said he did not beneficially own any shares as of June 30, 2025.
points: Where his money is: he indirectly owns about 19% of the adviser (through Dhandho Holdings), which earns the 0.90% fee, and he gets distributions from it. He also earns a salary and performance fees from Dalal Street, which runs the private Pabrai Investment Funds. Those private funds hold many of the same companies, and the fund documents say his funds own more than 20% of Gimat.
The documents do not say how much of his own wealth sits in the private funds, so his total personal exposure to these same stocks cannot be read from the ETF filings.

Neither the website, the FAQ, the investor presentation nor the 2025 and 2026 shareholder reports mention a personal investment amount. The adviser's regulatory brochure says only that the adviser, its employees or related persons 'may hold an interest in the ETF'.
Trustees: none owns any ETF shares, and trustees and officers as a group own under 1% (as of Sep 30, 2026).

good: Distinct portfolio. Several writers say the holdings are hard to replicate: international value, mostly outside the US, with zero overlap with the S&P 500. (Bezek, Seeking Alpha; ETF Central)

Pedigree and process. A manager who describes himself as a student of Warren Buffett, with a stated discipline of buying great businesses cheaply and holding them for a long time. Supporters like the willingness to hold cash and to hold winners. (Binary Tree Analytics, Seeking Alpha; the fund's own materials)

Cheaper and simpler than the old mutual fund. The ETF costs 0.90% against 1.00%–1.25% net before, with better tax efficiency and intraday trading. The adviser's own presentation and the information statement make this case.
Recent results. 28.90% for the year to June 30, 2026 against 22.32% for the S&P 500, and 30.14% for 2026 through October.
Steady inflows. Data sites show net inflows over the last one and three months and assets roughly doubling in 2026 (about $150 million in March to about $300 million).
bad: The fee. At 0.90% the fund costs far more than index funds (VT is 0.06% on ETF Database's comparison page) and more than the 0.69% average ETF Database shows for its segment. Ian Bezek, a former hedge fund analyst writing on Seeking Alpha in June 2026, called the fee relatively high and said it is only justified if the unique portfolio delivers, which he doubted. He rated the fund bearish.
Concentration and key-man risk. 20 positions and the top ten at 67%, with the prospectus saying the fund would liquidate without Pabrai.
Country and sector bets. Nearly 30% in Turkey, large energy and offshore-drilling exposure, and cyclical coal, all of which can fall together. India and Kazakhstan add governance and currency risk.

Track record. It still trails the S&P 500 since inception (16.91% a year against 21.83% at Oct 31, 2026), and the ETF itself is under a year old. Binary Tree Analytics noted the short history and said it would watch risk-adjusted results.

Trading costs. ETF Database lists an average bid-ask spread of 3.22% and a median premium to NAV of 0.47% with a historical maximum of 1.87%. Treat that as one data point; I could not check how current it is. Use limit orders, as the sponsor's own deck advises.
Promotional material. The ETF Central article on the fund reads as sponsor-written and does not list fees; the valuation claims in the investor presentation are the manager's own.
opinions.note: What I could not find: I searched for Reddit, Bogleheads, Morningstar, Barron's and WSJ commentary on the fund and none came back readable, so the views above come from the two Seeking Alpha articles, ETF Central, ETF Database, the adviser's own documents and the SEC filings. The fee criticism is the main theme found; I did not find anyone arguing the 0.90% fee is low.

history.title: History: the Pabrai Wagons Fund (mutual fund), Sep 29, 2023 to Feb 6, 2026
intro: The Pabrai Wagons Fund opened on September 29, 2023 as a mutual fund run by Mohnish Pabrai with the same approach as today's ETF: a concentrated portfolio of a few high-conviction holdings, anywhere in the world. It had two share classes, Retail (WAGNX) and Institutional (WGNIX). Retail carried a 0.25% 12b-1 fee and a 0.10% servicing fee, Institutional the 0.10% servicing fee only, and both charged a 1.00% fee on shares sold within 90 days. The adviser capped expenses at 1.25% (Retail) and 1.00% (Institutional) net; before the cap they were 1.84% and 1.59% in the year to June 2025.

It started small: net assets were $32.4 million at June 30, 2024 and $78.9 million at June 30, 2025 (both classes). Brokerage platforms held nearly all of it; at Sep 30, 2025 Vanguard Brokerage held 52.96% of the Institutional class, Schwab 21.19% and National Financial Services 20.74%. The largest single position was an Indian financial company, Edelweiss, at about 20% of the fund when it was bought.
perfRows: NAV rose from $10.00 to $12.47. Expense ratio after waiver 1.01%.
NAV fell from $12.47 to $10.69. Distributions of $0.15 a share ($0.14 of capital gains). Turnover 69.25%.
A very large swing for a fund with about 20 holdings.
After taxes on distributions 9.92%; after distributions and sale 7.82%.
history.perfNote: In short: a strong first nine months, a deep drawdown in early 2025, and a recovery that still left it well behind the S&P 500 at the end of 2025. On the Aug 20, 2025 call Pabrai said the fund had badly underperformed the index in its first two years, more than he would have expected, and that since early 2025 it had roughly kept pace. He argued many of the holdings take five or more years to pay off, citing Reysas, held since 2019, which went three or four years with little return despite a wide discount.
why: Growth. The fund and adviser said the ETF would reach more investors. Pabrai said the mutual fund would not be profitable for the adviser until about $150 million of assets (he said the fund was about $80 million in August 2025). The documents do not tie the conversion to that number, but it shows why growth mattered.

Tax efficiency. ETFs can meet redemptions by handing over shares instead of selling them, which usually means fewer capital-gains distributions. The mutual fund had paid $0.14 a share in capital gains for the year to June 2025. The fund's FAQ says the ETF also uses tax-loss harvesting.

Lower and simpler cost. One 0.90% fee replaced the 1.25% (Retail) and 1.00% (Institutional) net expense ratios, and the ETF drops the 1.00% short-term redemption fee. The information statement shows $92 a year on $10,000 for the ETF against $127 for Retail and $102 for Institutional, and says the adviser could not recoup earlier fee waivers from the ETF.

Trading and transparency. Intraday trading at market prices, and daily holdings disclosure. The FAQ says Pabrai spent most of a 28-year career running private funds for institutions and the ETF extends the strategy to a broader audience.

What shareholders gave up, which the information statement also lists: the ability to redeem directly at NAV, and brokerage costs and bid-ask spreads when trading. ETF shares can also trade above or below NAV.
how: The Trust's board unanimously approved the reorganization. No shareholder vote was needed.
Pabrai announced it on the quarterly call.
The Retail class closed and was merged into the Institutional class.

Last day to buy or redeem mutual fund shares. Holders without a qualifying brokerage account were cashed out around Feb 2 to 5, which could be taxable (and carried a 10% withholding for direct IRA holders).
The ETF took over the mutual fund's assets, accounting and performance history, intended as a tax-free reorganization.
WAGN began trading on the NYSE. A June 18, 2026 press release announced the transfer to NYSE Arca.
history.after: Since the conversion the record has been much better (28.90% for the year to June 30, 2026 against 22.32% for the index) and assets have roughly doubled to about $300 million. The documents do not say the conversion caused either; the period also coincided with strong gains in his energy and coal holdings.

calls.title: Sep 23, 2026 shareholder call: what Pabrai said
calls.intro: Summary of the full 16-page transcript you supplied. Pabrai answered one question per holding, then a few fund-wide ones, and said he ran out of time. The summary is in my words, not his, and he gave no figures beyond those noted. The call date is Sep 23, 2026, so weights and prices he cites are as of then.

items.p: Across the Wagons Fund, his private funds and related entities he owns about 30% of Reysas Logistics and a little over 12% of Reysas REIT. He said a founder hinted years ago that he was uncomfortable with a stake above 30%, so he voluntarily capped Logistics at 30%; that cap is why WAGN holds little of it. He said Logistics is the cheaper bet, trading below the value of the REIT shares it owns, and he would own more if free to. In WAGN, about 15% of assets is Reysas REIT and about 3% to 4% is Reysas Logistics (a little under a fifth of the fund together). He called Reysas his highest-conviction idea and said he would sell only if the family sold. His case rests on the founder's son Egemen's energy and creativity, with examples: a former Tata factory in Turkey (over 1 million square feet) being redeveloped into warehouses, and a government-matched organic tomato farm for export to Germany. He also said he may do a podcast on this.

He called the two similar but said Warrior is the better business and deserves the larger allocation. Warrior is all longwall mining, has mines closer to the port and can ship by barge or rail, so he estimates it pays the railroad under half of what Alpha pays. Alpha has a single railroad to the port, and he said the railroad takes roughly a quarter of the coal price, up to about $60 a ton. Alpha's reserves are in effect near-endless because it runs many small mines that become viable at higher prices. He likened Warrior to Aramco: near the bottom of the seaborne cost curve.

He agreed debt is a concern but said Transocean's management dislikes it and has cut it sharply. He praised the equity issuance at about $3 a share. He expects the Valaris merger to close in the fourth quarter, with Brazil's approval expected, which would cut leverage further. He said management told him the top goal is taking debt to zero and that he expects asset sales without a fire sale. He expects leverage to be a non-issue by the end of 2027 and acknowledged going 'out on a limb'.

He has owned both for almost ten years. Nuvama was spun out of Edelweiss. He sees Indian financial services as early-stage, comparing it with the US around 1980 to 1982, and likened the bet to buying Schwab then.

He agreed airports like TAV are not comparable to Heathrow or Paris and that geopolitics (the Ukraine and Iran wars) has hurt. Tailwinds: low-cost carriers at Antalya, Ankara, Izmir and Almaty use gates efficiently, and the aircraft-delivery squeeze should ease. In Almaty, TAV gave up fuel income earlier than planned in return for much higher per-passenger fees, which he expects to show up in 2027 results. TAV is paying out cash and may buy more assets.

He is disappointed that the founder owns under 1%. The issue is his pay, not his stake. He has urged him, last year and again this year, to raise his pay and find a way to give himself shares or options, and has seen no movement. He is not worried, calling the founder a servant leader who is not money-motivated.

He met senior management in Athens for the first time within the last couple of weeks, and his view of the company rose. He began buying in the $70s to $80s a share less than a year ago; the stock is now more than twice that and still deeply below net asset value in his view. He cited low-cost, light-covenant ship financing through Japanese special purpose vehicles that most shippers cannot get. Calling it a special company, not a typical Greek shipper.

Not part of a broader emerging-markets theme; he said he is opportunistic, as with Danaos. The bet is on the founder and the cash returned to investors. Kaspi owns 92% to 93% of Hepsiburada in Istanbul and he expects it to take it private eventually. He visited Hepsiburada and said founder Mikhail spends about 40% of his time in Turkey, teams in Istanbul and Almaty are sharing products, and the Hepsiburada app is already improving. He expects clearer results in one to three years.

Constellation: sad about Mark Leonard's health, which led him to leave the board, but he said Leonard's culture is firmly built in. Tab Gida: he expects GLP-1 drugs to hurt it in Turkey as elsewhere; he is excited about its Doner brand in China and urged management to copy Chipotle; it is one of his lowest-conviction holdings. Mongolian Mining: sold because Mongolian government factions want to revisit the mining deal terms, which he called an existential threat he could not handicap. He still liked the business (surface coal mine, and a gold side that did far better than designed, with gold at about $5,000 an ounce).

On recommending Berkshire over the fund for young investors: he will not use podcasts to promote products he has a stake in, and said an S&P 500 holder with liquidity could do better in Berkshire. On cyclicals versus compounders: he rejects the labels, calling Warrior his Aramco and Reysas REIT a compounder, not a REIT. On minority shareholders at Kaspi and Gimat: he has no concern about unfair treatment. On inflows to the ETF: he and his team decide where each day's new money goes (which positions, how much) based on conviction and position limits, and he has felt no discomfort so far.

calls.note: The transcript's own disclosures say the Predecessor Fund started Sep 29, 2023, the ETF succeeded its Institutional Class, history before Feb 6, 2026 is the predecessor's, and the ETF began trading on NYSE Feb 9, 2026.

calls.title: Jun 10, 2026 shareholder call: what Pabrai said
calls.intro: Summary of the full 16-page transcript you supplied. About 25 questions were chosen from 100 to 125 submitted. In my words, not his.

items.p: Asked why WAGN holds about twice as much Warrior as Alpha. Both are shareholder-focused, but Warrior uses longwall mining, which is cheaper, sits in the bottom quartile of the global cost curve, and can reach the port of Mobile by rail or barge. Alpha depends on a single railroad that takes a percentage of revenue. He put Warrior's cost to the port at $15 to $30 a ton and Alpha's at roughly $25 to $60. He said Warrior would rank higher even if it paid only dividends. Warrior was barred from buying back stock until Apr 19, 2026 because of its tax loss carryforwards, so buybacks could join dividends once its cash balance rises, perhaps in a quarter or two.

Transocean, Noble and Valaris together were over 19% of the fund (the question said about 17%). He said capital-intensive businesses can be excellent (Micron, FlightSafety, BNSF) if bought well below replacement cost, and has no plan to exit soon. He cited the thesis that the last drillship ever built by humans has already been built. He called the Transocean and Valaris deal a big win-win with little spread, and said Transocean's management would run the combination.

P/E is the wrong lens because of non-cash goodwill charges. On free cash flow the multiple is nowhere near 20 or 40 times. Organic growth has been about 3% a year, which he thinks deserves a cash-flow multiple somewhere in the middle of 10 to 17 times. The second engine is buying businesses at about 4 or 5 times cash flow, a 20% to 25% reinvestment return.

The company has no real investor disclosure, and nudges to provide an investor deck have mostly been ignored. He is fine with that because the father-son team are exceptional capital allocators who want returns of 20% to 30% or more. He warned that he mostly gives the bull case and that some holdings will lose.

He corrected the question: buying began 10 to 11 months earlier, in 2025, not 2024, and across everything he manages he owns over 25%, not 20%. At purchase the market cap was about $70 million to $80 million, and the real estate alone was about $70 million. He called it partly a venture-style bet on growing beyond two stores, compared it to Walmart and See's Candies, and said that not adding would have been a cardinal sin. The market cap is now over $300 million.

TAV: he said the headwinds are mostly unrelated to the Iran war: Pratt & Whitney engine groundings, Boeing delivery shortages and very low per-passenger fees at Almaty, which the government is helping raise. He expects these to ease in two to three years. Kaspi: a good management team replicating its Kazakhstan playbook in Turkey, with WeChat recently taking a stake. The dividend was reinstated and yields about 10%. He sees Turkey as a moonshot on top of a business he paid a fair price for. Edelweiss: Nuvama's market cap now exceeds Edelweiss's, an IPO of its EAAA asset-management arm is planned in months, but one of two co-CEOs there recently left, which he called not good news; the thesis remains intact.

The fund never held it; he fully exited before the mutual fund started in Sep 2023. It was his largest US bet for six years (2017 to 2023) and roughly doubled. He sold in 2023 when Samsung turned aggressive on market share and the oligopoly's rationality looked broken. He has no regrets about the sale and no plan to buy at current valuations, but regrets exits such as Ferrari, Goldman Sachs and BYD.

He said he once overdosed on Graham and underdosed on Munger, and since about 2017 to 2018 (Nick Sleep's influence) he does not sell at fair value and may sell only far above it. He rejected the cyclical versus compounder labels using Aramco and Warrior as examples. He named Constellation as the top management team and Kaspi as the likely second. He said ETF rules do not force trimming winners that rise in value. He will be at the Pareto Energy Conference in Oslo on Sep 16. On Warrior and Alpha price spreads: High Vol A is oversupplied by Warrior's volumes, and he expects the spreads to normalize in a year to 18 months. On distributions: as a regulated investment company the ETF must distribute in December, including nearly all dividend income and net realized gains, and holders can reinvest through their broker.

calls.note: Mohnish's remarks are paraphrased. Any weights or prices are as of Jun 10, 2026.

calls.title: Mar 11, 2026 shareholder call: what Pabrai said
calls.intro: Summary of the full 21-page transcript you supplied. It was the first call after the ETF began trading on the NYSE. He said he prioritized newer positions. In my words, not his.

items.p: He rejects the buckets, using Saudi Aramco (all-in cost under $12 a barrel, about 12 million barrels a day) as an example of a low-cost producer that rarely loses money. The PLV index was about $220 a ton, roughly its seven-year average and, adjusted for inflation, near a floor, with several Central Appalachian mines closing as cash-flow negative. At $220 for a full year he put Warrior at over $550 million of cash flow (market cap under $5 billion) and Alpha at over $350 million (under $3 billion), which he said he would sign for.

His degree is in computer engineering and he ran an IT firm for over a decade, but software was usually too expensive. Constellation fell from about $5,500 to the low $2,000s. He argued AI helps incumbents in vertical-market software: more founders may sell, acquisition multiples (historically 4 to 5 times cash flow) could fall, and costs may drop. He said no portfolio manager escapes a high miss rate (Buffett had about 12 decisions that moved the needle). On Topicus: similar DNA, a less competitive European market, nothing he does not like.

Kaspi: a 'heads I win, tails I do not lose much' bet. The price fell after a dividend cut tied to buying a Turkish fintech and bank; Turkey is seven or eight times Kazakhstan's market and far less digital; the founder is 'a total rock star'. Gimat: he will not be an activist. Across all entities he had just crossed 25% ownership (a filing that week). It has two stores and is venture-like, with downside protected by an entry at a modest valuation and real estate it plans to monetize.

He called Transocean's acquisition of Valaris a stroke of genius: leverage falls because Valaris is underlevered, a larger footprint improves contract negotiations, and Transocean is the stronger operator. The deal had not yet closed.

Warrior's tax loss carryforward rules cap any holder at 5% and block buybacks until Apr 19, 2026 (he owned about 4% across entities). Alpha cut its fully diluted share count about 32% over four years (2022 to 2026) and has under 12 million shares left. He sketched a scenario in which only about 8 million shares can be bought, Alpha reaches about $180 and then turns into a dividend payer, possibly over $250 a share in seven or eight years, about $1 billion a year. He cited India's steel demand rising around 2028 to 2029 as the supply-demand turn, said nothing so far has invalidated his coal thesis, and said what he watches is shares outstanding in 2035.

Reysas: no investor relations or deck. He cited exceptional capital allocation (investments need a 25% to 35% annual return), productivity like Greg Abel's, and creativity (rooftop solar, a small German apartment venture). Footprint is about 12 million square feet, going to about 23 million in three years. TAB Gida: Burger King and Popeyes master franchisee in Turkey; revenue is in lira, which he accepts because the team is a 'jockey bet' (civil engineers who beat McDonald's), though it is not a hard-currency earner like TAV.

Exited OXY, auto dealers and homebuilders because they were his lowest-conviction ideas, replaced by higher-conviction ones (opportunity cost). On converting to an ETF: in hindsight, he might have started as one, citing lower frictional costs, lower fees and access to non-US investors. He said he expects to beat the S&P 500 over the long term, with no guarantee, and expects the S&P's heavy Magnificent 7 weighting to struggle over 10 to 15 years. He declined thermal coal (Core Natural Resources) because of the Iran war. Investors from India and Canada can buy; some European and other countries are restricted; the investor-relations manager can confirm the list.

He said Turkey felt like the US in the 1960s: investors overweight macro and underweight micro, and 'micro trumps macro'. He said Reysas's market cap was about $15 million when he first visited versus $600 million to $800 million of liquidation value (2% to 4%). TAV is mostly hard-currency (euro) revenue and about 46% owned by the French government.

calls.note: Paraphrased. Figures are as he stated them on Mar 11, 2026.

calls.title: May 14, 2025 shareholder call (mutual fund era): what Pabrai said
calls.intro: Summary of the full 17-page transcript you supplied. This was the mutual fund (Pabrai Wagons Fund), before the ETF conversion. In my words, not his.

items.p: Net assets were about $66 to 67 million. He said the fund needs about $150 million to cover all internal and external costs and was not yet profitable. Roughly $75 to 76 million had been sent in net since launch, so the fund was worth about 10% to 13% below money in, and much of that money came in the last few months during the market drop. He said net inflows had come almost every day for months. For redemptions, the fund keeps a seven-figure cash balance and can ask for same-day settlement. In 18 to 19 months only two or three days (under 1%) had redemptions exceeding subscriptions and cash, and only a small part of one security had to be sold. The fund held 15 to 20 positions.

On a question about Alpha's buybacks at $215 to $400 a share when the stock was near $120: he had no disagreement with management and said they were smart to stop buying and keep about $450 million in cash while losing about $30 to 40 million a year at depressed coal prices. His case rests on the end state, not the path: if Alpha shrinks from 12 to 13 million shares to about 3 million in 20 years while earning $1 billion to $1.5 billion a year, that is roughly $500 a share of cash flow. He said a business producing $500 million a year for 50 years that costs $2 billion needs no spreadsheet. He called Warrior his favorite met coal bet: a low-cost operator that was not losing money in a trough, and would be lower still once Blue Creek came online. He hoped coal prices stayed depressed (ESG selling) so the companies could buy back more cheaply.

Edelweiss was then the largest position. He said he avoids levered financial firms, but most of Edelweiss's lending is in run-off, and most of its businesses are not lending. Its market cap was about $1 billion versus about $2.5 billion for the Nuvama wealth business it had spun out. An IPO of the alternative-asset business (EAAA), which he compared to Brookfield or Blackstone with higher growth in India, was expected within a quarter. He expects four or five spin-offs in four or five years and wants to keep the spun-off shares. India-listed stocks can now be bought like US ones.

He said the bet is bottom-up, not on Turkey. TAV earns mostly euros and has lira costs, so inflation is a tailwind. Reysas's warehouses (land, concrete and steel) are inflation-indexed, and over six years the lira lost over 80% while Reysas's intrinsic value in dollars doubled or tripled. He agreed with Buffett's remark on weak currencies in most cases, but not all.

The offshore group (Valaris, Noble, Tidewater) emerged from restructuring with little debt. He said replacement cost could be five to ten times market cap, new drillships would need day rates 50% to 100% higher, offshore is 25% to 35% of world oil, and offshore all-in costs of $30 to $50 a barrel beat shale. He said Noble traded at about five times non-peak cash flow with a dividend yield approaching 10%. On OXY: he likes Vicki Hollub but prefers simpler, smaller businesses.

Danaos was not sold after a quarter; it falls outside the top 10 that is disclosed in some months, so it only looked sold in the filings. The same applies to Coca-Cola Icecek. Car dealers: avoids Carvana over the promoters' ethics; he likes dealers with new-car franchises since profits come from parts and service. Tariffs: a net negative for equities; he made no tariff-based changes. Japanese trading houses: too hard. Mutual fund motive: to reach more investors than his private funds. Time horizon: at least five years, citing Sequoia's early underperformance. Non-US investors: interest was strong, and an ETF structure might be the way to serve them, which is what later happened.

calls.note: Paraphrased. Figures are as he stated them on May 14, 2025.

calls.title: Mar 19, 2025 semi-annual call (mutual fund era): what Pabrai said
calls.intro: Summary of the full 12-page transcript you supplied. More than 160 questions were submitted; he answered a small fraction. In my words, not his.

items.p: Asked how he explains losing all gains since inception, he said the fund optimizes for long-term performance, not for smoothing volatility, and he does not hedge. He said auction-driven stock markets overshoot both ways, unlike property markets. The night before, Istanbul's mayor had been arrested, Turkish markets and the lira fell sharply, and all of the fund's Turkish positions lost money, but he saw little long-term impact on their value.

At the end of 2024 each was about 15% to 16% of the fund, together about 31%; he said Edelweiss was then over a fifth of the portfolio. He said they were the two highest-conviction ideas. Edelweiss had a market cap of about $1 billion and was about to list its alternative-assets arm at an expected $1 billion to $1.5 billion. He expected about four listings over four or five years, roughly one a year. TAV: he called its management among the best he had met, and described the Almaty airport (bought for about $300 million, with expected EBITDA possibly over $200 million a year), and said both companies trade at a small fraction of intrinsic value.

He said all the coal holdings are metallurgical coal, not a short-term bet on prices above $300. His argument: new blast furnaces last 40 to 70 years, met coal supply is scarce and slow to bring on, and a company valued around $2 billion could produce well above $600 million in cash in many years. He sold Core Natural Resources (a mix of thermal and met coal) to hold a pure met portfolio, keeping Warrior and Alpha (AMR).

items.h: Why some holdings left the top 10
items.p: Anadolu Efes fell out after Russia took over the assets of its Russian brewing joint venture on Dec 31, which he moved to the too-hard pile. He also explained the fund's structure: half the portfolio must have at least three stocks, none above 25%; the other half can have no position above 5%, typically about 4%. That implies at least 16 stocks, and positions near 4% may or may not make the reported top 10.

Car dealers: the market misjudged moats (EVs adopt slower than assumed, will mostly still sell through dealers, and parts and service stay profitable). He called Asbury, AutoNation and Group 1 well run and said he would rate Penske (PAG) higher, but paid for value instead. Homebuilders: the big ones are taking share from small builders, going asset-light like NVR, using central manufacturing, and buying back stock. Reysas: he said a founder's body language implied a preference that the stake not be increased, so Reysas will not be a big WAGN position. He cannot project 10 to 20 years because the father is in his mid-60s.

Mutual fund rules force baskets; he would prefer one coal bet, one dealer and one builder. The fund would need several billion dollars to cut its expense ratio materially; fees were capped and the adviser was subsidizing the fund. A tax-efficient ETF was raised by a questioner, and he said nothing then beyond that the expense ratio might be revisited. The disclosures list gross expense ratios of 4.74% (WAGNX) and 4.22% (WGNIX) against net 1.25% and 1.00%, with a 0.90% cap through at least Oct 31, 2025, and a 1.00% redemption fee within 90 days.

He called OXY one of his lower-conviction bets, a bet on CEO Vicki Hollub. He recommended the book 'Buffett and Munger Unscripted'. He said calls might turn quarterly so more questions can be answered.

calls.note: Paraphrased. Figures are as he stated them on Mar 19, 2025.

calls.title: Sep 18, 2024 semi-annual call (mutual fund era): what Pabrai said
calls.intro: Summary of the full 13-page transcript you supplied, the fund's second semi-annual call, nearly a year after launch. In my words, not his.

items.h: Opening: the fund as of mid-2024
items.p: As of June 30, 2024 the fund held 27 securities across Turkey, the US, Canada, Europe, China and Mongolia, with the top five over 45%. Four core allocations made up 94%: Turkish holdings (Coca-Cola Icecek, Anadolu Efes, TAV), US coal, a few US car dealers and US homebuilders. Performance since the Sep 29, 2023 inception to Aug 31, 2024: retail class +21.54%, institutional +21.86%, against +33.5% for the S&P 500. He said the fund led the index six weeks earlier and fell behind in August, which he called temporary. He noted the S&P 500's trailing P/E of 27.2 versus 25.6 in Sep 2000 and said the portfolio's was 7.5. The fund was on Vanguard, Interactive Brokers and Pershing, with Fidelity and Schwab pending.

The top three positions at the end of June were all Turkish (TAV, Anadolu Efes, Coca-Cola Icecek), exactly 33% together, and among his highest-conviction ideas. On capital-flow or political risk, he said much of the revenue is earned outside Turkey and ring-fenced: TAV's non-Turkish airports and euro-denominated contracts, Anadolu Efes's beer volumes in Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere, and Coca-Cola Icecek's volumes outside Turkey. On boycotts at Coca-Cola Icecek, he said they are hard to handicap, he would not sell because of them, and he praised the brand, management and the CEO. He described the Uzbekistan bottling deal (about $300 million for about $20 million of pretax earnings, now over $100 million) and a small chance that Coca-Cola Icecek could get part of India.

He said the coal businesses were priced as if they would go out of business, are net cash for the first time in their histories, and are stress-tested. The Australian premium low-vol index was about $185 a ton (recent low $176); around 10 million tons of capacity outside his holdings was underwater and likely to shut, and mines that close do not come back quickly (equipment lead times of two years, no workers, no capital). He was surprised by the Arch and CONSOL merger but liked it: a combined company of about $5 billion market cap would, in his estimate, make about $500 million of cash in a bad year and over $1 billion in a good one, with buybacks the only use of cash.

Nvidia: outside his circle of competence. At a $2.8 trillion market cap and roughly $60 billion of annual cash flow he would need to believe in much larger cash flows, and compared it to Schlumberger in the 1980s. OXY: a placeholder with a low downside, under 4% of the fund, run by Vicki Hollub. The fund needs about 15 or 16 positions at least (realistically 20 to 30), and he said he cannot find that many ideas. Homebuilders: not as cyclical as thought, a US shortage of over 5 million homes, big builders have lower capital costs and move toward the NVR model; Tri Pointe bought back more than half its shares in a few years. Danaos: his only Greek position, with cash flows locked in by long charters.

calls.note: Paraphrased. Figures are as he stated them on Sep 18, 2024; performance and weights are from that date.
